projects.title: Overcurrent relay coordination study
projects.summary: Settings and time grading for ten IDMT relays on a 230 kV generation and transmission system, with a MATLAB application for the curves.
projects.problem: Ten overcurrent relays protect three generators, their step-up transformers and the 230 kV lines of a 7-bus system. Each needs a pickup and time setting that clears its own faults first and backs up its neighbour.
projects.objective: Calculate the plug setting, time multiplier setting and operating time of relays R1 to R10, verify selectivity, and plot every time–current curve in a MATLAB App Designer interface.
approach: Normal currents from the bus loads (60, 75 and 85 MVA at 230 kV) and the given three-phase fault levels at each bus.
CT ratios from 150/1 to 3000/1; pickup at 1.2 to 1.5 times normal current; upstream pickup at least 1.2 times downstream where the network allowed.
IEC Normal Inverse characteristic, t = TMS × 0.14 / (PSM^0.02 − 1), with a 0.2 to 0.4 s coordination interval.
A literature review of how distributed generation, CT saturation and bidirectional flow disturb overcurrent coordination.
specs: 0.30 s, 0.30 s, 0.70 s and 0.80 s on the four lines
results: Primary operating times from 0.30 s (R10) to 1.31 s (generator relays).
Every primary and backup pair separated by 0.3 to 0.8 s.
Maximum calculation error of 1.00% between the application and hand calculation.

images.alt: Single-line diagram of the 7-bus system with relays R1 to R10 and their CT ratios

projects.title: Phase and earth-fault protection of an 11 kV network
projects.context: Switchgear and Protection open-ended lab, APU
projects.summary: Simulink model of a 33/11 kV radial microgrid with phase and earth-fault relays tested under four fault types and six inverse curves.
projects.problem: A radial 11 kV network fed from a 33 kV grid needs overcurrent protection that trips selectively and still clears a fault when the primary relay fails.
projects.objective: Build the network in Simulink with overcurrent relays on the distribution lines, then compare relay characteristics and fault types.
approach: 33 kV source, delta–wye transformer to 11 kV, three buses with PQ loads, CTs and circuit breakers.
Relays with separate phase (50/51) and earth (50N/51N) units, set to six IEC and IEEE inverse curves in turn.
Single-line-to-ground, double-line-to-ground and three-phase faults on line 2; a backup test with the primary relay disabled.
specs: IEC NI, VI, EI; IEEE MI, VI, EI
results: Trip times from 0.21 s (IEEE Extremely Inverse) to 0.47 s (IEC Normal Inverse) for a line-to-ground fault.
Backup relay tripped at 0.47 s after the primary's 0.27 s signal: the 0.2 s interval held.
Asymmetrical faults tripped both phase and earth units; the three-phase fault tripped the phase unit only, as expected with no zero-sequence current.

images.alt: Simulink model of the 33/11 kV radial network with relays and breakers
Relay block settings with IEC Normal Inverse selected for phase and earth protection
Scope traces of voltage, current and trip signals during a fault

projects.title: Power flow analysis of a 10-bus network
projects.context: Power System Analysis open-ended lab, APU
projects.summary: Newton-Raphson, Gauss-Seidel and Fast-Decoupled solutions in MATLAB and PowerWorld, with a 35 MW load increase.
projects.problem: How does a 10-bus network's voltage profile and loss change when load grows at two buses?
projects.objective: Model the network in MATLAB and PowerWorld Simulator, solve it with three methods and compare the base and loaded cases.
approach: Bus and line data entered in MATLAB scripts for each solver; the same network built in PowerWorld.
Base case solved, then 35 MW added at Buses 3 and 6.
results: Newton-Raphson converged in three iterations.
Base case: all voltages within limits, total active loss 6.15 MW.
With 35 MW added: Bus 3 fell to 0.969 pu and losses rose to 9.80 MW.

images.alt: PowerWorld one-line diagram of the 10-bus network
MATLAB output of bus voltages and line flows

projects.title: Self-supervised Vision Transformer for PCB defect detection
projects.summary: Automated PCB inspection with a self-supervised Vision Transformer and a detector, optimised for GPU inference.
projects.problem: Manual inspection of printed circuit boards is slow and labelled defect data is scarce.
projects.objective: Classify and locate PCB defects with a model pre-trained without labels, then run it fast enough for an inspection line.
approach: Self-supervised pre-training (SimCLR) of a MaxViT-Small backbone; RF-DETR and DINOv2 for detection.
Export to ONNX Runtime with CUDA for GPU inference; Streamlit interface showing detections.
specs: ONNX Runtime with CUDA on an RTX 3060 laptop GPU
results: 77.50% test accuracy and a weighted F1 score of 0.8281 across 22 component classes.
68.83% mAP@50 and 53.12% mAP@50–95 for detection with RF-DETR.
37.25 frames per second (26.85 ms average latency), above the 30 FPS real-time target.

projects.title: Residential smart parking system
projects.context: Microprocessor Systems and Embedded Software group assignment, APU
projects.summary: Group design for an automated, tray-based car park. Badr built the tray: an Arduino robot that carries the car and avoids obstacles with a servo-scanned ultrasonic sensor.
needsInput: Your own part of the team work
projects.problem: Drivers lose time and fuel searching for a space, and manual car parks give no guidance.
projects.objective: Design a fully automatic parking system that moves a car to a space with no driver involved. The group split it into a tray system, a lift system, and spot detection with assisted parking.
approach: Simulated the tray in Tinkercad first: an Arduino Uno, an ultrasonic sensor mounted on a servo, an L293D motor driver and two DC motors.
Built the prototype tray with an Arduino Uno, ultrasonic sensor, servo motor and an IR sensor that reads the surface under the tray.
Wrote the control program in the Arduino IDE (C/C++): the servo sweeps the ultrasonic sensor from 0° to 180° to scan ahead, left and right.
When an obstacle is closer than 5 cm, the tray stops and turns towards the side with more space.
Used the serial monitor to watch the sensor readings and tune the behaviour.
specs: Ultrasonic sensor on a servo; IR surface sensor
L293D motor driver, two DC motors

projects.title: Medicine identification and obstacle detection for the hospital AGV
projects.context: Group design project, APU: individual part
projects.role: Individual part of a four-member team
projects.summary: Badr's part of the hospital AGV: two vision models on a Jetson Orin Nano, one to identify the medicines being carried and one to detect obstacles and judge their distance.
projects.problem: A hospital delivery robot must confirm it carries the right medicine, and must see people, beds and trolleys in a corridor and know how far away they are.
projects.objective: Select the vision hardware, prepare the datasets, train the two models and test them before they run on the robot.
approach: Chose the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano over a Raspberry Pi 4 for its GPU, and the ZED 2i stereo camera over a USB webcam because it measures depth.
Took four public datasets from Roboflow Universe (two of hospital scenes, two of medicines), unified their labels, and built one project for navigation safety and one for medicine recognition.
Trained a segmentation model for 50 epochs at batch size 4 to fit a 6 GB GPU, and a YOLOv8s medicine detector on 360 images for 100 epochs at batch size 8, both with early stopping.
Built a medication test interface with a "Sniper Mode" that crops the centre 640 × 640 of a 1920 × 1080 frame to mimic a focused check, with a confidence slider.
Built a navigation interface that reads the ZED 2i depth at each detected object and sets a safety state from its distance.
Planned the software in layers: the two ONNX models sit above the GPU drivers on the Jetson, with Python classes on top.
projects.sources: OneDrive > University > Year 4 Sem 1 > 02. GDP > Brainstorming > Report Drafts > New > GDP Report most updated.docx, "Chapter 2 Badr Albdulmajeed TP061632 Individual Part".

projects.title: Baby carrot freshness inspection
projects.context: Machine Vision and Intelligence group assignment, APU
projects.role: Freshness inspection (vision and AI), Tkinter GUI integration, and report formatting/writing; four-member group project
projects.summary: Baby carrots graded fresh, aging or spoiled two ways: an OpenCV pipeline reading texture, dark spots, mould and colour, and a Roboflow object-detection model trained on 281 annotated frames, both run from one Tkinter app.
projects.problem: Manual freshness checks on produce are slow and inconsistent. The team had to inspect baby carrots for freshness, ripeness and disease, and classify them, using both a vision-based and an AI-based method.
projects.objective: Detect fresh, aging and spoiled baby carrots in camera video with a rule-based vision method and with an AI model, and bring the team's inspection tasks into one application.
approach: Recorded baby carrots at three stages, fresh, aging and spoiled, with the lab camera in MVS, then split the videos into frames with OpenCV.

Vision method: Laplacian variance for surface roughness, a grayscale threshold to count and size dark spots, an HSV mask for mould, and HSV colour to tell bright orange from dull; each carrot is boxed and labelled.
AI method: annotated 281 frames in Roboflow, trained a Roboflow 3.0 object-detection model, and ran it over the video in Python with boxes, labels and confidence scores.

Built the team application in Tkinter: pick a member's task and a vision- or AI-based method, open the camera or a file, and watch results live; video runs in its own thread so the window does not freeze.
Fixed lag during live AI inspection by synchronising frames instead of processing each one as it arrived, and retuned the HSV values and lighting after glare and shadows broke detection.
specs: 640×640; 3 outputs per training example; rotation between −15° and +15°
results: Roboflow model: mAP 99.2%, precision 98.5% and recall 98.6%. These are object-detection evaluation percentages reported by the model dashboard, not classification accuracy, latency or physical measurements.
All 281 images are frames from the team's own recorded videos, so these scores describe that footage rather than new carrots.
The vision method sorted carrots into fresh, aging and spoiled and improved with each round of HSV and lighting changes, though it was not perfect.
The application ran freshness and disease inspection, vision- and AI-based, from a live camera or a file; ripeness and classification were not delivered.

images.alt: Carrot inspection app running the Roboflow model: fresh, aging and spoiled carrots boxed with confidence scores
Vision-based output: carrots labelled fresh, aging and spoiled from colour, spots and texture
Roboflow dataset: 281 images split 235, 30 and 16, resized to 640×640

limitations: The 281 images are extracted frames from the team’s own videos: 235 training, 30 validation and 16 test images. Nearby frames may be correlated. The report does not establish a video-disjoint split or testing on independent new carrots, so generalisation to new produce, cameras or lighting is unverified.

The dashboard reports mAP 99.2%, precision 98.5% and recall 98.6%. It does not identify the mAP IoU/averaging setting or clearly name the evaluation partition, so these must not be presented as independently verified test-set performance or a production guarantee.

The task-distribution table assigns Badr freshness inspection, GUI integration and report formatting/writing. The disease component was a teammate’s work integrated into the group application; ripeness and classification were not delivered. No individual ownership of the whole group system is claimed.
Previously listed as “Fruit inspection”; the original project URL is retained. No source code screenshot or private Roboflow credential is published.
sources: Machine Vision and Intelligence group report: task distribution on PDF page 7, freshness work on pages 7–19, dashboard and dataset figures on pages 17–18, and GUI/integration discussion on pages 40–44.

projects.title: Honeycomb modular power hub
projects.summary: Product design for a repairable power strip: a master hub with hexagonal socket modules that snap on magnetically, so one failed socket is replaced on its own. Modelled in SolidWorks.
projects.problem: A standard power strip is thrown away whole when one socket or its wiring fails, which adds to e-waste, and overloaded strips are a fire risk.
projects.objective: Design a power hub that allows socket-by-socket replacement, includes fast charging, and can be arranged around a desk.
approach: Generated three concepts by brainstorming and a morphological chart: the Honeycomb Hub (modular cluster), the Articulated Snake (flexible strip) and the Vertical Stacking Tower.
Scored the concepts against the design objectives and selected the Honeycomb Hub, noting that it is the harder one to manufacture.
Designed a master hub that plugs into the wall and passes AC power to each hexagonal module through magnetic pogo-pin connectors.
Modelled every module as a separate part in SolidWorks, mated them into the assembly, and produced the engineering drawing.
projects.sources: OneDrive > University > Year 4 Sem 2 > PCT > WORD DRAFTS > Badr word > Tp061632 PCT.docx, "Modular Smart Power Hub: The Honeycomb System", submitted 12 June 2026.

projects.title: Transformer and alternator testing
projects.summary: Ratio, open-circuit, short-circuit and load tests on a single-phase transformer, and characteristic tests on a three-phase alternator.
projects.objective: Measure the transformation ratio, find the iron losses and excitation parameters, find the winding resistance and reactance, and determine voltage regulation and efficiency.
approach: Transformation ratio test: measured primary and secondary voltage at five settings from 51.5 V to 181.6 V.
Open-circuit test with the high-voltage winding open, recording voltage, no-load current and power for the core losses.
Short-circuit test with the low-voltage winding shorted, raising the voltage slowly up to full-load current.
Load test to calculate efficiency and voltage regulation.
Second lab: resistance test on a three-phase alternator to find its armature resistance, and its characteristics.
results: The measured transformation ratio stayed at about 1.22 across all five voltage settings.
projects.sources: OneDrive > University > 02. EM2 > tp061632 EM2 assignment.docx, submitted 10 Aug 2023.

projects.title: Microgrid with solar PV and battery storage
projects.context: Generation, Transmission and Distribution assignment, APU
projects.summary: Simulink microgrid with PV, battery state-of-charge control and household and commercial loads, plus power-factor correction.

images.alt: Simulink model of the microgrid with PV, battery and loads

projects.objective: Build and simulate a microgrid with solar panels, battery storage and varying loads, and work out the power-factor correction it needs.
approach: Modelled the grid connection, the PV panels, the battery subsystem and the loads in Simulink.
Monitored real and reactive power, voltage, frequency and the battery state of charge during the run.
Took the real and reactive power from the simulation and calculated the capacitor compensation needed to reach a power factor of 0.98.
results: Simulated load: 4,212.5 W and 4,003.8 VAR, a power factor of 0.724.
Reaching a power factor of 0.98 needs about 3,144 VAR of capacitive compensation.

projects.title: Off-grid wind and battery power conversion
projects.summary: Rectifier, buck-boost converter, 48 V battery and PWM inverter sized and simulated in Simulink for a 500 W off-grid wind turbine.
projects.problem: Wind does not blow steadily, so an off-grid home needs power electronics and storage between the turbine and its appliances.
projects.objective: Design and simulate a complete off-grid wind energy system from the turbine to the AC output.
approach: Sized the system for Malaysian conditions, assuming an average wind speed of 3 m/s.
Chose a full-bridge rectifier to turn the turbine output into DC, and a buck-boost DC-DC converter to regulate it.
Sized a 48 V, 100 Ah battery with 80% usable depth of discharge from the household daily energy use.
Added a PWM inverter for a 230 V AC sine output and built the whole chain with its controls in Simulink.
results: The simulation showed a stable DC bus voltage, a working battery storage stage and a usable AC output.
The report lists power quality, efficiency and real-world testing as work still to do.
specs: Horizontal-axis, 500 W, cut-in 2 m/s, rated 10 m/s
projects.sources: OneDrive > University > Year 3 Sem 2 > PED > A > Assingment > Ped Tp061632 .docx, submitted 12 Jan 2025.

projects.title: Speech enhancement filter app
projects.summary: MATLAB app that loads a recording, applies a chosen filter, and lets the user see, hear, compare and save the cleaned speech.
projects.problem: Background noise in streets, restaurants or factories makes recorded speech hard to understand.
projects.objective: Create a speech enhancement system in MATLAB that uses filters to remove noise and improve speech quality.
approach: Built a graphical app: the user uploads an audio file, picks a filter, and views the signal and its frequency content before and after.
Included seven filters: low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, band-stop, Butterworth, Chebyshev and Wiener.
Added playback of the original and filtered audio, saving of the result, and side-by-side comparison of two filters.
Added messages for a missing file or no filter selected.
results: The app filtered the test recordings and let the filters be compared by graph and by ear.
specs: Low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, band-stop, Butterworth, Chebyshev, Wiener
projects.sources: OneDrive > University > Year 3 Sem 2 > DSP > ASSIN > Sound test > Tp061632 DSP Speech enchancment.docx, submitted 2 Jan 2025.

projects.title: Discrete-time system with the Z-transform
projects.context: Signals and Linear Systems open-ended lab, APU
projects.summary: MATLAB study of a discrete-time system defined by a difference equation: its output, frequency spectra, and impulse, step and frequency responses.
projects.objective: Complete a MATLAB script that investigates a discrete-time system defined by a difference equation.
approach: Applied an input signal with 10 Hz, 20 Hz and 30 Hz components and computed the system output.
Plotted the frequency spectrum of the input and of the output to compare their frequency content.
Computed the impulse response, the step response and the frequency response of the system.
Varied the equation coefficients (A1, A2, A3) to see how they change the response.

projects.title: FM modulation and demodulation
projects.summary: Simulink model that frequency-modulates a sine wave, passes it through a noisy channel and demodulates it, compared at signal-to-noise ratios of 30 dB and 10 dB.
projects.problem: How well does frequency modulation carry a signal once the channel adds noise?
projects.objective: Perform FM modulation and demodulation of a sinusoidal signal in Simulink, and analyse the result when an AWGN channel is added at different signal-to-noise ratios.
approach: Built the chain in Simulink: sine-wave information signal, FM Modulator Passband block, AWGN Channel block, FM Demodulator Passband block, with scopes and spectrum analysers at each stage.
Set the modulator and demodulator to the same carrier frequency and frequency deviation so the signal could be recovered.
Ran the model with the channel set to 30 dB and then 10 dB, and compared the spectrum, the modulated signal and the demodulated output.
results: At 10 dB the demodulated output showed clearly more distortion than at 30 dB.
projects.sources: OneDrive > University > Year 3 Sem 1 > 01. CEP > Assingment > TP061632 CEP (FM).docx, submitted 19 Aug 2024.

projects.title: Temperature control for a batch reactor
projects.summary: Proposed closed-loop temperature control for a steam-jacketed batch reactor, alongside a separate simulated Arduino monitoring and alarm demonstration in Tinkercad. The demonstration alarms above 37.5 °C; it does not establish control of a physical reactor or steam valve.
projects.problem: A batch reactor's temperature sets how fast the reaction runs and how pure the product is, so it has to stay in range as heating and cooling loads change.
projects.objective: Design a monitoring and control system for the reactor's temperature and show how its sensor, controller and actuator work together.
approach: Proposed process-control arrangement: a Fieldbus temperature transmitter reports to the temperature controller; its 4–20 mA output is converted by a transducer to a 3–15 PSI signal for an air-to-open steam valve on the reactor jacket.
Worked out the controller action: with an air-to-open steam valve, a rising temperature must lower the controller output, so the controller is set to reverse action.

The separate Arduino/Tinkercad demonstration described in the report reads a TMP36 temperature sensor in °C and °F and includes distance/motion sensing, LCD indications, a buzzer, warning LED and motor behaviour in its example code.

In that demonstration code, above 37.5 °C the buzzer and LED switch on and the motor stops; the report also describes a 30 cm proximity condition and a motion alert. This is monitoring/alarm logic rather than demonstrated closed-loop temperature regulation.
specs: Arduino Uno for the monitoring/alarm demonstration; a separate process controller is proposed for the reactor
TMP36 temperature, ultrasonic distance, PIR motion
4–20 mA from the controller, 3–15 PSI to the valve

images.alt: Tinkercad circuit: Arduino Uno with a TMP36 temperature sensor, a 16×2 LCD, two push buttons and three LEDs on a breadboard

needsInput: Confirm the LabVIEW front panel and block diagram in the report are your own before showing them (they may come from the referenced paper)
Simulation result or screenshot of the running Tinkercad circuit
limitations: The steam-jacketed reactor, Fieldbus transmitter, controller, I/P transducer and pneumatic valve form a proposed process-control arrangement. The provided evidence does not demonstrate an implemented or commissioned physical reactor loop, set-point tracking or control-performance measurements.

The implemented educational demonstration is a simulated Arduino temperature monitor and alarm in Tinkercad. Its circuit figure does not establish every peripheral mentioned in the example code. LabVIEW material remains listed as part of the source record; authorship and independent implementation of those diagrams have not been established, so they are not presented as verified original experimental results.
sources: Sensors and Actuators assignment (DOCX), Tinkercad circuit/code section and process-control discussion/conclusion; source paragraphs 70–106.

projects.title: Two-level library lighting design
projects.summary: Lighting scheme for a client's two-storey library refurbishment in DIALux evo 11, simulated with and without daylight and checked room by room for lighting power density.
projects.problem: A client renovating a small library wanted a new lighting scheme that meets lighting standards and looks good, while using less energy and money without lowering the quality of the light.
projects.objective: Model the library from the client's floor plan and design an energy-efficient lighting scheme for every room and hall on both levels.
approach: Built both storeys, 124 m by 76 m, in DIALux evo 11 from the client's plan, with rooms, windows, doors, materials and furniture.

Level 1 holds a meeting room, kitchen, librarian room, checkout desks, history room, washrooms and the main reading hall; level 2 adds a second meeting room, a computer lab, a mechanical room and storage.

Chose luminaires by task: RZB Less is More Flex PRO LED strips light the bookshelves, Philips BY121P LED luminaires give general light in the reading halls, and Philips RC136B, RS772B, SM400C and RC463B luminaires light the rooms.
Simulated every space with and without daylight, then summed fixture power and worked out daily energy and lighting power density for each room.
Painted the reading halls a soft peach yellow to help readers concentrate, with red carpet throughout and tiles in the washrooms.
specs: Library schedule: 14 hours a day; some source room calculations instead use 8 hours
12 SG, 310 RZB and 45 Philips BY121P luminaires
results: Report’s simulation/design calculation — Level 1 hall: 6,840 W over 7,511.93 m², a lighting power density of 0.91 W/m² and about 95.76 kWh a day.
Report’s simulation/design calculation — Level 2 hall: 0.90 W/m² over 8,168.10 m² with 53 Philips BY121P and 300 RZB luminaires.
Report’s simulation/design calculation — Rooms from 1.05 to 2.28 W/m²: checkout desks 1.05, history room 1.45, librarian room 1.57, mechanical room 1.59, meeting room 1 2.28.

images.alt: DIALux evo render of a lit bookshelf aisle in the reading hall
Level 1 reading hall with daylight
Meeting room 1 lighting render
History room with daylight
History room without daylight, lit by its luminaires only
First-floor layout seen from above in DIALux evo

limitations: The stated powers, areas and lighting power densities are retained from the report’s DIALux design, not field measurements or independently verified lighting-standard compliance. LPD is installed power / area (W/m²); daily energy is power × operating time (kWh/day).

Meeting room 1 reports 325.2 W and 3.76248 kWh. The report mixes 8-hour and 14-hour schedules: 325.2 W × 8 h = 2.6016 kWh and × 14 h = 4.5528 kWh. Neither gives its stated energy value. The reported 2.28 W/m² is retained.

For the computer lab, the source reports 528 W, 227.96 m², 2.32 W/m² and 7.9456 kWh for 14 hours. Arithmetic gives 7.392 kWh; 528 / 227.96 ≈ 2.316 W/m² already rounds to 2.32. Its later “around 7 fixtures” recommendation puts operating hours into an LPD calculation and is dimensionally inconsistent; it is not adopted as a redesign.

Other unresolved daily-energy discrepancies: the checkout room reports 5.482 kWh but 356 W × 14 h = 4.984 kWh; the librarian room reports 2.5395 kWh but 127.5 W × 14 h = 1.785 kWh. Original reported figures are not silently replaced with these arithmetic cross-checks.

The Level 1 hall’s 6,840 W, 7,511.93 m², 0.91 W/m² and 95.76 kWh at 14 hours are mutually consistent to the stated rounding. The Level 2 hall’s reported 0.90 W/m² and 8,168.10 m² remain as source results.
sources: Electrical Power Utilisation lighting assignment report, DIALux design figures and power/energy calculations on PDF pages 21–27.

projects.title: Bumper car with laser tag
projects.role: Team project (four members): concept chosen by the group
projects.summary: Bumper car concept that doubles as laser tag, driven by two joysticks. The group chose Badr's sketch and modelled the full car in SolidWorks.

projects.problem: A standard bumper car has a front steering wheel that a rider can hit in a rear collision, and the ride offers nothing beyond bumping.
projects.objective: Each member proposed a bumper car concept; the group then selected one and produced its engineering drawings and 3D assembly.
approach: Sketched a concept with an infrared beam and a receiver on each car, so riders score points as in laser tag.
Replaced the steering wheel and pedals with a 360° joystick on each side of the seat, with buttons to fire the beam and change settings.
Added safety features: a four-point seat belt, an adjustable headrest, an emergency button, a circuit breaker and air vents against overheating.
The group chose this sketch and combined it with the spring bumper from another member's concept.
Modelled the parts in SolidWorks, produced the engineering drawings with bills of materials, and built the assembly step by step: seat and belt, joysticks, wheels, bumper, then the full car.
results: The group selected this concept as its final design.
Delivered the full SolidWorks assembly with isometric, exploded and section views.
projects.sources: Engineering Design group assignment "Bumper Car", Group 9, submitted 19 Feb 2021 (PDF supplied by Badr): concept on pages 3-4, chosen design on page 8, views on pages 83-85.

projects.title: Wheatstone bridge with a potentiometer
projects.summary: Balanced and unbalanced Wheatstone bridge simulated in Multisim: the unknown arm found from the bridge ratio, and the output traced from −1.6667 V to 378.79 mV as one arm changed from 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ.
projects.problem: How does a Wheatstone bridge reveal an unknown resistance, and how does its output move away from zero as one arm changes?
projects.objective: Build the bridge from three fixed resistors and a potentiometer, show the balanced and unbalanced conditions, and compare the simulated output with the Thevenin equation.
approach: Derived the balance condition R4 = (R2/R1)·R3 and, from Thevenin's theorem, the unbalanced output VBD = V(R3/(R1+R3) − R4/(R2+R4)).
Multisim balanced case: R1 = R2 = 1 kΩ with R3 set from 2 kΩ to 10 kΩ, and the potentiometer tuned until the simulated output read 0 V.
Unbalanced case: 5 V supply, R1 = R2 = 1 kΩ and a 5 kΩ fourth arm, with the potentiometer stepped from 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ in 1 kΩ steps.
results: Simulation result — Balanced: the calculated unknown resistance matched the simulated value at all five settings, from 2 kΩ to 10 kΩ, with 0 V across the galvanometer.
Simulation result — Unbalanced: the output rose from −1.6667 V at 1 kΩ through 0 V at 5 kΩ to 378.79 mV at 10 kΩ, matching the equation at every step.

images.alt: Multisim bridge with the potentiometer at 1 kΩ, reading −1.6667 V
Multisim bridge balanced at 5 kΩ, reading 0 V

limitations: These are NI Multisim Live simulation readings and analytical calculations, not physical bench measurements. Agreement and the displayed 0 V balance apply to the reported model and numerical precision; hardware tolerance, noise and instrument uncertainty were not established.
sources: Instrumentation and Measurement report, final 4.pdf, PDF pages 3–11; cross-checked against the overlapping Wheatstone report Lap Report1-19.pdf.

projects.title: Inverting and non-inverting 741 amplifiers
projects.summary: 741 op-amp amplifiers simulated in Multisim with three resistor pairs each: inverting gains of −1, −1.3333 and −0.8571 and non-inverting gains of 2, 2.3333 and 1.8571, all matching the calculated values.
projects.problem: How closely does a 741 op-amp follow the ideal gain equations in its inverting and non-inverting forms?
projects.objective: Build both amplifiers, read the gain from the input and output waveforms, and compare it with −Rf/R1 and 1 + Rf/R1.
approach: Derived the closed-loop gains from nodal analysis and the virtual-short principle: −Rf/R1 for the inverting amplifier and 1 + Rf/R1 for the non-inverting one.
Simulated both circuits around a 741 with a ±12 V supply and a 1 V, 50 Hz sine input in Multisim, plotting simulated input and output together.
Ran three resistor pairs for each: equal (1 kΩ and 1 kΩ), larger feedback (3 kΩ and 4 kΩ) and smaller feedback (7 kΩ and 6 kΩ).
results: Simulation result — Inverting: gains of −1, −1.3333 and −0.8571, with the output 180° out of phase with the input.
Simulation result — Non-inverting: gains of 2, 2.3333 and 1.8571, in phase with the input.
Simulation result — Simulated and calculated gains agreed at every setting, with 0% error in the simulator.

images.alt: Multisim inverting amplifier with 3 kΩ input and 4 kΩ feedback resistors, output in antiphase with the input
Multisim non-inverting amplifier with 3 kΩ and 4 kΩ resistors, output in phase with the input

limitations: The report states 0% error between its displayed simulated and calculated gains. This is a rounded simulation comparison, not a measured zero-error claim about a physical 741. Offset, resistor tolerance, noise and hardware frequency response were not verified.
sources: Instrumentation and Measurement report, final 4.pdf, amplifier experiment and results on PDF pages 13–22, including the tables on page 19.

projects.title: Two-port network parameters
projects.summary: Z- and Y-parameters of resistive T and π networks found from simulated open- and short-circuit tests in LTspice at 5, 10 and 15 V, showing the network is reciprocal.
projects.problem: Can a two-port network's Z- and Y-parameters be found from measurements at its terminals alone, and do they hold as the test voltage changes?
projects.objective: Build T and π networks, measure the port voltages and currents under open- and short-circuit tests, and calculate the parameters.
approach: T network for the Z-parameters: drove one port with the other open, recording I1 and V2, then I2 and V1, at 5, 10 and 15 V.
π network for the Y-parameters: drove one port with the other shorted, recording I1 and I2 at the same three voltages.
Built both networks from 1 kΩ, 2 kΩ and 3 kΩ resistors and calculated each parameter from the measured voltage and current ratios.
results: Z-parameters: z11 = 3000 Ω, z12 = z21 = 2000 Ω and z22 = 5000 Ω at all three voltages.
Source report, Table 4: Y-parameters: y11 = 0.0015 S, y12 = y21 = 0.0005 S and y22 = 0.000833 S.
z12 equals z21 and y12 equals y21, so the network is reciprocal. This reciprocity statement does not resolve the current-reference sign discrepancy.

images.alt: LTspice π network at 5 V with its operating-point currents

limitations: The report draws both port currents entering the positive-voltage terminals (PDF page 3, Figure 2; pages 6–7, Figures 9–10). For its π network, I1 = V1/1000 + (V1 − V2)/2000 and I2 = V2/3000 + (V2 − V1)/2000. Under that convention, y12 = y21 = −0.0005 S; y11 = 0.0015 S and y22 ≈ 0.000833 S.

Table 4 reports positive transfer values, +0.0005 S, which are retained above as the original source results. Their magnitudes match the circuit; their signs do not match the drawn entering-current convention. Reporting magnitudes or an opposite ammeter reference could explain this, but the report does not reconcile it. No simulator rerun or physical measurement is claimed.

The sample y22 calculation on PDF page 10 prints 0.00833 S, whereas 4.16667 mA / 5 V ≈ 0.000833 S agrees with Table 4. Its y11 prose also says 2 mA while its fraction uses 15 mA. These are unresolved source transcription discrepancies.
The T-network Z tests and π-network Y tests use separate resistor arrangements. They are not claimed to be equivalent networks or inverse parameter matrices.
sources: Analysis of Circuits report, PDF pages 3–10 and LTspice appendix pages 11–16.

projects.problem: High-voltage equipment must survive short overvoltages from lightning and switching, and DC test voltages must be generated with low ripple.
projects.objective: Study how the circuit parameters shape an impulse waveform, and how load current, frequency and capacitance affect ripple and voltage drop in multiplier circuits.
approach: Impulse generator: varied the front resistor, tail resistor and the two capacitances one at a time and recorded peak voltage, front time and tail time.
Voltage doubler: recorded ripple voltage while varying load current, supply frequency and capacitance.
Three-stage Cockcroft-Walton multiplier: recorded ripple and voltage drop for the same three variables.
specs: 15 kV charging voltage, 0.6 µF, 0.001 µF, Rf 15 Ω, Rt 115 Ω, 5 cm sphere gap
results: Default impulse: 27.76 kV peak, 0.5 µs front time and 50.5 µs tail time.
Raising the tail resistor lengthened the tail time from 33.0 µs to 101.0 µs; raising the front resistor from 15 Ω to 75 Ω lengthened it from 50.5 µs to 74.0 µs.
Voltage doubler: ripple rose from 500 mV to 2,540 mV as load current rose from 5 µA to 25.4 µA, and fell from 1,000 mV to 200 mV as frequency rose from 50 Hz to 250 Hz.
Cockcroft-Walton multiplier: raising the stage capacitance from 0.1 µF to 2.0 µF cut the ripple from 3.0 V to 0.15 V.

projects.objective: Measure the voltages at no load, and the current and voltage of the line under matched, ohmic-inductive, pure inductive, ohmic-capacitive and pure capacitive loads.
approach: Built the circuit from a three-phase supply, circuit breaker, three-phase transformer and the transmission line model.
Recorded the line voltages with no load connected.
Connected a matched resistive load, then mixed and pure inductive loads, then mixed and pure capacitive loads, recording current and voltage each time.
results: At no load the receiving-end voltage was higher than the sending-end voltage, because of the line capacitance.
Pure inductive loads gave high reactive power and low efficiency.
Adding capacitance improved the power factor.

projects.objective: Find the open-circuit characteristic from a no-load test, and the load characteristic and voltage regulation from a load test.
approach: No-load test: raised the field current in steps and recorded the generated voltage.
Load test: added lamp loads in steps and recorded terminal voltage against load current.
Calculated the voltage regulation from the load-test readings.
results: No-load voltage rose from 115 V at 160 mA of field current to 142 V at 300 mA.
Terminal voltage fell from 220 V at 1.2 A to 176 V at 12.7 A of load current.
Voltage regulation calculated as 22.91%.

projects.problem: Unbalanced loads make a washing machine drum vibrate, which wears the machine and makes it unreliable.
projects.objective: Model the machine, simulate its response, and choose a controller and sensor that reduce the vibration.
approach: Derived a transfer function for the Samsung WF0804 under normal load from real system values.
Simulated the open-loop response in MATLAB/Simulink; it was under-damped, with overshoot and a long settling time.
Added a PID controller and a voice coil actuator in a closed loop and tuned the gains.
Compared the response with and without the controller, and used a root locus plot to study the pole locations.
results: The PID controller reduced the overshoot and improved the settling time.
The report notes that the response still needs further tuning and suggests adaptive control as the next step.

projects.summary: Transfer-function model of the vibration of a washing machine under unbalanced load, with a PID controller and voice coil actuator simulated in Simulink.

projects.objective: Build suitable IIR and FIR filters and analyse discrete-time signals in the frequency domain.
approach: Generated a test signal with three frequency components.
Designed Butterworth IIR filters with buttord and butter: a high-pass filter (pass above 150 Hz, stop below 100 Hz) and a band-stop filter for 150–200 Hz.
Designed the matching FIR filters with fir1 and a Hamming window, at order 34.
Plotted the filtered signals and the magnitude and phase responses of each pair.
results: The IIR filters gave a sharper cutoff with fewer calculations, but distorted the phase.
The FIR filters kept a smooth phase, but needed more coefficients.

projects.objective: Design a digital circuit that performs at least three operations to solve an algebraic equation, using the fewest universal gates and showing the result on seven-segment displays.
approach: Chose the expression (A + B) + √(B²) and wrote its truth table.
Drew a Karnaugh map for each display segment and simplified the logic.
Built the circuit in simulation from 74LS00 NAND gates and 74LS02 NOR gates, with a 74LS49 decoder driving the display.

projects.summary: Logic design that evaluates an algebraic expression of binary inputs using only NAND and NOR gates, with a seven-segment display for the answer.
projects.limitations: The report records that the simulated circuit displayed only the digits 7 and 8; no working result is claimed on the site.

Added saving of the plotted waveform as a PNG file as the extra feature.
